en: Preface to the *Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* (contained in the *Collected Works of Lingguo Sijujing* and the *Yuan’an Ji*).

In the winter of the Xinsi year of the Hongwu era, as the imperial court was nearing the completion of its carving of the Tripitaka—comprising the Sutras, Vinaya, and Shastras—it issued an edict to the Office of Buddhist Registrars (*Senglusi*).
Regarding all the texts of the *zong* (sectarian) vehicle, those that are most essential have been compiled according to their respective lineages.

[Your servant] So-and-so respectfully examines that, during the Jingde era of the Song dynasty, the monk Daoyuan of Wu compiled the *Chuandeng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) in thirty fascicles.
Emperor Zhenzong specifically commanded Yang Yi, the Hanlin Academician, and others to edit and preface it; it was titled the *Jingde Chuandeng lu*. From this point onward...
The Chan school flourished greatly. It is traditionally said that those who attained the Dharma became increasingly numerous.
During the Tiānshèng era of Emperor Rénzōng, Lǐ Zūnxū, the Prince Consort (Fùmādūwèi), compiled the *Guǎngdēnglù*.
At the beginning of the Jiànzhōng Jìngguó era, Chán Master Báisè of Fógúo compiled the *Xùdēnglù*. In the tenth year of the Chūnxī era, Chán Master Míng of Jìngcí compiled the *Liándēnghuìyào*.
During the Jiatai era, Chan Master Leian compiled the *Pudeng Lu*. At the end of the Song dynasty, the monk Dachu Jin of Lingyin observed that the previous five *Denglu* records were somewhat prolix;
he therefore condensed them into the *Wudeng Huiyuan*. I venture to say that the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* is the ultimate work;
as for the four subsequent lamp records, how could they avoid the fault of omitting this while retaining that? [The] compilation...

The original was written as a book; its intent was certainly virtuous. However, it failed to honor the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp from the Jingde Era) as an unalterable canon and instead took [other materials] to compile them therein, which resulted in redundancy.

Now, by the grace of encountering Your Majesty’s sagely brilliance and being able to gloriously assist the Buddha-vehicle, I have ventured to forget my presumption and compiled the *Xu Chuandeng Lu* (Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp). As for its lineage of transmission...
The sequence begins from the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp Compiled during the Jingde Era) and starts with the several generations following Great Mirror (Huineng).

It was compiled by Chan Master Fenyang Shanzhao, who linked the lineages down to the several generations of Master [Name], concluding the record. In total, there were [number] generations, yielding [number] realized persons.

Among them, [number] individuals whose recorded encounters and dialogues were extant were included. This work is titled the *Xùchuándēnglù* (Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp). In total—

It consists of thirty-six fascicles. As for the sources from which it was compiled, they include the *Wudeng Huiyuan*, the *Fozu Haiming*, the *Sengbao Zhuan*, the *Fen deng lu*, as well as the various charts of the Chan lineage and the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of the patriarchs.

In assembling these texts, I have maintained their original form, making only slight adjustments in selection and omission; I did not dare to engage in arbitrary pruning or polishing that would compromise their authenticity. Its...
In this world, we exclusively highlight the Great Mirror (Dajian) above and dare not allow it to be split by the five lineages.
This is because these five lineages mutually stimulate and inspire one another, yet all originate from the Great Mirror; therefore, this Continued Record unifies and integrates them.

This is because they all return to the same source. Alas! The Dharma of the mind is formless; it cannot be obtained from others. Its value lies in silent resonance and self-realization through awakening.
When Bodhidharma came from the East, he pointed directly to the source of the mind, established no reliance on words and letters, and taught that by awakening to the mind, one becomes a Buddha.

What, then, is the use of speech? Nevertheless, the mental dharma pervades all places; the great earth, mountains, rivers, grasses, trees, tiles, and pebbles are all manifestations of one's own mind, and each serves as a gateway for triggering awakening—how much more so, then, are speech and writing?
Indeed, although the unsurpassed, wondrous Way cannot be transmitted through language, it can be perceived through language;
for language serves as the guiding mark that points toward the mind. Therefore, students often take language as the criterion for gauging the depth of their realization.
Thus, although the Buddhas and Patriarchs say that there is nothing to transmit, at the moment of bestowal and reception, they are like a needle meeting its eye.
The words and phrases [of these masters] were surely intended for specific occasions and circumstances, as were their verses of certification (*pramāṇa-gāthā*).
If one were to take them up merely to transmit them to future generations, they would all suffice as resources for awakening. How could they be discarded and not transmitted?

Thus, was it not because the various masters of antiquity were so earnest regarding the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) that it provided such benefit to both the doctrine and the school? [Your servant], [Name], with limited learning and knowledge...
I am common and mediocre, yet I have been unworthily honored with the charge of presiding over the teaching; thus, having received this mandate, I am filled with trepidation and find no peace.

Therefore, I have gathered my students and selected from the various scriptures, arranging them according to their historical lineages. As for those phrases and dialogues concerning spiritual capacities and karmic conditions for which there is no source from which to verify or correct them, [they remain as they are].
It remains to be completed by future colleagues who shall carry on this work.
